title: The Recursive Symmetric Group and Myhill's Theorem
content:
This file is a child of schroeder-bernstein-oq-03, the formalization of Myhill's isomorphism theorem — the computability-theoretic analogue of Schröder–Bernstein. Where classical Schröder–Bernstein builds a bijection from two injections A ↪ B and B ↪ A, Myhill's theorem upgrades this to the effective setting: from two computable one-one reductions it produces a computable permutation of ℕ (a bijection e with both e and e.symm computable, Mathlib's Equiv.Computable), witnessing that the two sets are recursively isomorphic. The full construction proceeds by a back-and-forth priority argument, still open in the parent file.

This entry isolates the structural fact that the priority construction silently depends on and that stands on its own: the computable permutations of ℕ form a subgroup recSym of the symmetric group Equiv.Perm ℕ — the classical recursive symmetric group of computability theory. Composition-closure is precisely what licenses a back-and-forth argument to chain finitely many computable adjustments and remain computable. The file then shows every transposition, and hence every finitely-supported permutation, lands in recSym, and that recSym is nontrivial. All results are 0-axiom (no sorry, no added axiom, no native_decide).
mathContext: A permutation $e \in \operatorname{Sym}(\mathbb{N})$ is *computable* iff both $e$ and $e^{-1}$ are computable functions $\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$. Myhill: computable reductions $A \le_1 B$ and $B \le_1 A$ imply a computable permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ carrying $A$ to $B$ — the effective Schröder–Bernstein. This file proves $\mathrm{recSym} = \{e : e,\,e^{-1}\text{ computable}\}$ is a subgroup of $\operatorname{Sym}(\mathbb{N})$.

title: Transpositions are Computable
content: The concrete computability input to the whole entry. primrec_swapFun exhibits the swapping function x ↦ if x = m then n else if x = n then m else x as primitive recursive: it is an ite-tree whose guards are the decidable equality tests x = m and x = n, built with PrimrecRel.comp Primrec.eq. computable_swap_coe transports this to the coercion of Equiv.swap m n through swap_apply_def, and swap_computable finishes by observing (via symm_swap) that a transposition is its own inverse, so both halves of Equiv.Computable are the same computability fact.
mathContext: $\operatorname{swap}(m,n)(x) = \begin{cases} n & x = m \\ m & x = n \\ x & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$, an $\mathsf{ite}$-tree over decidable equality — hence primitive recursive — and self-inverse.

title: The Recursive Symmetric Group recSym
content: recSym is the subgroup of Equiv.Perm ℕ whose carrier is the computable permutations {e | e.Computable}. The three closure fields are each a one-line reduction to the symmetric-group operation laws: one_mem' rewrites Equiv.Perm.one_def and discharges both coordinates with Computable.id; mul_mem' rewrites mul_def (a * b = b.trans a) and applies Equiv.Computable.trans; inv_mem' rewrites inv_def (a⁻¹ = a.symm) and applies Equiv.Computable.symm. This packages Mathlib's Equiv.Computable predicate as a genuine group object — the recursive symmetric group of computability theory.
mathContext: $\mathrm{recSym} = \{\, e \in \operatorname{Sym}(\mathbb{N}) \mid e \text{ and } e^{-1} \text{ computable} \,\}$; closure under $1$, $\cdot$, and ${}^{-1}$ from $1 = \mathrm{id}$, $a\cdot b = b\mathbin{\text{≫}}a$, $a^{-1} = a^{\mathrm{symm}}$.

title: Transposition Generators and Finite Products
content: From swap_mem, closure propagates: closure_isSwap_le places the entire subgroup generated by all transpositions inside recSym via Subgroup.closure_le, and list_prod_swap_mem uses Subgroup.list_prod_mem to conclude that every finite product of transpositions is a computable permutation. Since the finitely-supported permutations of ℕ are exactly the finite products of transpositions, this delivers their computability with no extra work — the subgroup laws do all of it.
mathContext: $\langle\, \{\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ IsSwap}\} \,\rangle \le \mathrm{recSym}$, and $\prod_i \operatorname{swap}(m_i,n_i) \in \mathrm{recSym}$ for every finite list — in particular every finitely-supported permutation is computable.

title: Nontriviality of recSym
content: recSym_ne_bot shows the recursive symmetric group is not the trivial group: if recSym were ⊥ then swap 0 1 would equal the identity permutation, but evaluating both sides at 0 gives 1 = 0 (swap_apply_left sends 0 to 1, while the identity fixes 0), a contradiction. So recSym contains at least one nontrivial element.
